**Observation Log:**

- [TEMPORAL] Session Date: 2023/01/22 (Sun) 05:18
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Cross-examination is a foundation of the common law trial to expose flaws in evidence.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The aim of cross-examination is to damage the witness's credibility and elicit material favorable to the cross-examiner's case.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The limits of cross-examination are not easily defined and may lead to seemingly irrelevant questions.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The trial judge should allow counsel some leeway in cross-examination to test opposing witness evidence.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] A judge must contain cross-examination within reasonable limits in the interest of justice.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The effectiveness of cross-examination is due to its tactical value.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Wigmore claimed that cross-examination is the greatest legal engine for the discovery of truth.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] A High Court case held that a judge acted prematurely in barring a defendant from asking a police officer the cause of death of a fellow officer.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The officer's cause of death was later found to be relevant to the accused's claims and the investigation's reliability.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The rules for controlling evidence before the court can be hard to reconcile with the tactical value of cross-examination.
